own_scenes.family: Nueva York: Def Jam, Queens y la edad de oro
own_scenes.desc: Las mixtapes venían de las cintas de Herc, Flash y los Cold Crush, y en Nueva York las firmaban Kid Capri, Ron G, DJ Clue o Tony Touch. Curtis Jackson, apadrinado por Jam Master Jay y presentado por él a Sha Money XL, provocó con «How to Rob» (1999), donde planeaba atracar a las estrellas; tras «Ghetto Qu’ran» le dispararon nueve veces (2000) y Columbia lo despidió. Con Sha Money inundó la calle de mixtapes robando bases ajenas: sobrevivir lo convirtió en la historia. Guess Who’s Back? (2002) convenció a Eminem, que lo fichó con Dr. Dre (Shady/Aftermath): Get Rich or Die Tryin’ (2003) e «In da Club» devolvieron el gangsta al gran público como no se veía desde Death Row. Todos copiaron su modelo (DJ Drama, detenido en 2007 por sus Gangsta Grillz). G-Unit dejó escapar a J. Cole, que fichó por Jay-Z.

influences.name: G-funk: The Chronic, Death Row y Snoop Doggy Dogg

refs.q: He survived and he became the story, and then his lyrics and the shit he was saying was so powerful.
refs.para: Sha Money XL (producer, New York): When we started the mixtape process after he’s been shot and after he’s went through that whole process, there became a demand, because guess what? He survived and he became the story, and then his lyrics and the shit he was saying was so powerful.

refs.q: He would have been a great thing for G-Unit, but 50 didn’t see it.
refs.para: Sha Money XL (producer, New York): If I had the power, I would have did the same shit Jay did. I wouldn’t have let him out the room. When I had that chance with Bobby Shmurda, I didn’t let him out the room. When you’re ready to do deals, you’ve got to do them, and I knew that J. Cole was a superstar. He would have been a great thing for G-Unit, but 50 didn’t see it.
